title: China Import Watch
dek: China's crude buying: import volumes, sourcing shifts, teapot run rates, and what it means for sour barrel demand.

claims.text: OilPrice.com reported on Nov 10, citing Reuters reporting of official customs data, that China's crude oil imports rose in October to 41.94 million tons, about 9.88 million barrels per day (b/d), the highest since March and up 9.4 percent on September on a daily basis. Seaborne imports rose 12 percent from September, according to Kpler data cited in the report. October imports were still 13.3 percent below October 2025, and imports in the first ten months of 2026 were 15.1 percent lower than in the same period of 2025. Imports from Saudi Arabia rose markedly to 1.62 million b/d, in line with the Saudi monthly total a year earlier, after Chinese buyers had sharply cut purchases from the region earlier in the year, OilPrice.com said.

Reuters reported on Nov 10 that China's seaborne crude arrivals rose 12 percent from September to about 9.2 million barrels per day (b/d) in October, their highest since March, according to Kpler data, while Kpler and Vortexa recorded a surge in imports from Saudi Arabia, putting October arrivals at 1.6 million b/d and 2 million b/d respectively. Energy Aspects estimated that China's refinery throughput fell from September levels to 13.75 million b/d in October, Reuters said.

Reuters columnist Clyde Russell wrote on Nov 2 that Asia's crude oil imports recovered in October to 26.39 million barrels per day, up from 24.24 million in September and just shy of the 27.0 million average in the three months before the February 28 attack on Iran, citing Kpler data. Asia's imports sourced through the Strait of Hormuz rose to 7.42 million barrels per day in October, still well below the 13.06 million pre-war average, and arrivals from Russia rose to 3.50 million barrels per day.

Reuters columnist Clyde Russell wrote on Oct 20 that China crude imports are poised to rise to more than 10 million barrels per day in October, the most since the 11.79 million barrels per day recorded in March, citing Kpler seaborne arrivals estimated at 9.02 million barrels per day plus about 1 million barrels per day of pipeline imports from Russia and Central Asia. September imports were 9.03 million barrels per day, refinery processing was 13.99 million barrels per day, and the gap implied a stock draw of about 530,000 barrels per day.

China's crude oil imports fell 21.5 percent from a year earlier in September to 37.1 million tonnes, or 9.03 million barrels per day, customs data showed, though the daily rate edged up 1.1 percent from August, Reuters reported on Oct 14. Imports for the first nine months of 2026 totalled 357.97 million tonnes, or 9.57 million barrels per day, down 15.3 percent from the same period last year. September seaborne imports stood at 7.6 million barrels per day, down from 9.9 million a year earlier, according to Vortexa, with Iranian oil arrivals down to 0.5 million barrels per day.
claims.vintage: Data: Sep 2026 customs; published Oct 14, 2026; accessed 2026-10-19

claims.text: FGE NexantECA and Energy Aspects cut their fourth-quarter China crude import forecasts by about 400,000 b/d, now expecting 9.2 to 9.3 million b/d versus last year's average of 11.6 million b/d, OilPrice.com reported on Sep 30. September imports were expected near August levels, with the arriving cargoes bought when prices were in the $80s before Brent held above $100; August imports were still 23.4% below a year earlier, improved from June's decade low of 7.1 million b/d. OilPrice quoted FGE NexantECA's Samuel Kong saying no significant upside is expected as hefty premiums and record-high freight erode margins, and reported the teapots could start reducing runs as Iranian and Venezuelan supply dries up under US sanctions.

Goldman Sachs estimated China's seaborne crude net imports rose about 6 percent in September from August but stayed almost 3 million barrels per day below normal seasonal levels, and its models point to only about 600,000 barrels per day more total crude imports in the fourth quarter versus the third. The bank estimates a sustained 1 million barrel per day change in China's net crude imports over six months would shift Brent's fair value by about 4 dollars a barrel.

Kpler reported on Nov 12 that Chinese refiners are stepping up purchases of West African and Brazilian crude despite cheaper Middle East alternatives, as ample Gulf supply and falling tanker rates reshape competition for Asian demand. Kpler assessments put the landed value of Nigerian Agbami into Ningbo at a premium of $19.65 a barrel to the Dubai swap for late-November loading, down $11.95 a barrel on the week, leaving prompt Agbami cargoes about $4 a barrel more competitive than Abu Dhabi Murban into China, Kpler said.

Reuters reported on Nov 5 that several independent refiners in China's eastern Shandong province bought 8 million to 10 million barrels of November-loading West African crude in the previous week, while sellers of West African and Brazilian crude offered steeper discounts to Chinese buyers to offset high freight costs, intensifying competition with Gulf grades. Unsold December-loading cargoes of Oman, Murban and Iraqi crude from the previous trading cycle also pressured spot premiums, traders told Reuters.

OilPrice.com reported on Nov 9, citing Iran International reporting of leaked confidential correspondence and Iranian Oil Ministry sources, that Iran has been using oil terminals and storage facilities in China to ship its oil to its biggest buyer and keep sanctioned tankers operating despite US sanctions. Acting oil minister Hamid Bovard wrote that Iran's Foreign Ministry had negotiated buying port facilities and oil terminals in China to establish a hub for sanctioned Iranian crude, and that Tehran had also secured long-term leases on large storage facilities in several Chinese locations, OilPrice.com said. Ministry sources told Iran International that Iran has bought control of port facilities at three locations in China and stakes in docks in Shandong province, home to China's independent refiners, and that sanctioned vessels linked to Hossein Shamkhani transported the crude to the Iran-controlled facilities.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 28, citing Bloomberg trading sources, that Chinese refiners have bought West African and Brazilian crude for December delivery after Atlantic Basin freight rates eased from record highs, paying premiums of up to $20 a barrel over ICE Brent for grades including Equatorial Guinea's Ceiba, Angola's Saturno and Brazil's Mero. The same report said independent teapot refiners are hunting the cheapest available supply after the US blockade in the Gulf of Oman cut off their Iranian feedstock, and that competition with India has pushed up prices for Russia's ESPO grade.

Reuters columnist Ron Bousso wrote on Oct 22 that Saudi Aramco and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co have started selling some cargoes on a delivered basis to buyers in China and India, a sharp departure from the usual practice of selling crude at the point of loading, as Gulf producers offer large discounts to offset record freight and insurance costs.

Kpler data showed India remained the largest buyer of Russian crude in September at about 1.82 million barrels per day, but its intake fell roughly 29 percent from July as Chinese refiners stepped up purchases and tightened availability, HDFC Sky reported on Oct 14. China took about 1.49 million barrels per day of Russian crude in September, and Kpler's Sumit Ritolia said Chinese refiners have drawn more Russian barrels in recent months partly because of reduced access to Iranian crude, adding to competition for the available supply.

Kpler data cited by Reuters on Oct 6 showed China's imports of Iranian oil nearly halved in September from a year earlier to 590,000 barrels per day, the lowest since January 2023, and Iran exported no crude at all in September for the first time since Kpler began tracking flows in 2013. The volume of Iranian crude stored on vessels outside the blockade zone has more than halved to 45 million barrels from 100 million barrels in late July, Kpler said. Reuters also reported that Bloomberg found at least 50 tankers, mostly carrying Iranian crude, bottled up off China's coast, and that Russian ESPO was commanding a premium of almost $30 a barrel above Brent, pricing most independent refiners out of Russian barrels while state-owned refiners took most of the available Russian crude.

Reuters reported on Oct 6 that Chinese independent refiners stepped up purchases of crude from Iraq and Qatar for October and November delivery to replace dwindling Iranian supplies, as exports from other Gulf producers through the Strait of Hormuz recover. Three traders told Reuters the refiners bought at least 12 million barrels of Iraqi and Qatari crude from trading houses Mercuria, Totsa and Trafigura, with one estimating total purchases of 15 to 20 million barrels. The cargoes sold at premiums of $12 to about $20 a barrel to the ICE Brent benchmark on a delivered basis; most were Iraqi Basra Medium and Heavy, among the cheapest Middle East grades available. Buyers included Hongrun Petrochemical, Qicheng Petrochemical, Qirun Petrochemical, Hualong and Chambroad Petrochemical, and Hongrun and Shenchi Petrochemical also bought 3 million barrels of Qatar's al-Shaheen crude for early-November arrival. One trader told Reuters that Iraqi oil has become the new benchmark for China's independent refiners because supplies are ample and can be obtained quickly. The deals followed purchases of more than 20 million barrels of crude from West Africa, Canada and Colombia between late August and early September as Iranian supply dwindled after the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian vessels in July.

Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cut its November crude prices for Asia to six-year lows while raising them for northwest Europe, Reuters reported, closing a question the watch had carried into October. Aramco set November Arab Light to Asia at $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, down $3 from October, the widest discount since June 2020; Arab Medium and Arab Heavy to Asia were cut $5 a barrel. The cuts defied a Reuters survey expecting up to a $5 a barrel hike, and refining sources told Reuters they were aimed at compensating Asian buyers for record freight costs (VLCC Gulf to China at $1.2 million a day, per LSEG data) and protecting Aramco's market share after the war disrupted exports.

Russian and Iranian crude accounted for less than one-third of China's September imports, down from about half in August, as China shifted toward non-sanctioned supply, per Goldman Sachs analysis. The bank said the shift toward openly traded crude could make changes in Chinese purchasing more visible in benchmark pricing.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Fox News interview on Sep 27 that only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain on the water under the US blockade, with final deliveries to China expected within about two weeks, after which he claimed Iran would have nothing left to trade. That is an unverified prediction from the official directing the sanctions effort, not independent evidence that Iranian exports have stopped.

TankerTrackers reported Sep 24 that almost 6 million barrels of confiscated Iranian crude, including the 1.88-million-barrel tanker Majestic X seized in the Indian Ocean in April while headed for China, were crossing the Atlantic toward the United States. The report relies on a single tracking source and should be treated as a lead until corroborated.
claims.vintage: TankerTrackers report Sep 24, 2026; published Sep 26, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: Reuters reported on Nov 10 that China's refined oil product exports fell to 5.18 million tons in October from 7.16 million tons in September, while product imports rose to 3.15 million tons from 1.85 million tons. Product exports in the first ten months of 2026 totaled 46.59 million tons, down 2 percent from a year earlier, Reuters said, citing customs data.

Reuters reported on Nov 5 that China released a larger than expected fourth batch of fuel export quotas in the previous week, which raised expectations of increased refined product supply in Asia and weighed on regional refining margins.

Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire wrote on Oct 5 that China's suspension of fuel exports for October left India best placed to fill the resulting hole in Asian fuel supply. Citing Kpler data, he reported India has 23 refineries able to process about 5.6 million b/d and was the larger fuel exporter in 2025 (about 47 million tonnes of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel versus China's 25.4 million), though India's fuel exports in the first nine months of 2026 were down roughly 23%, or about 8 million tonnes, year on year. He noted two recent cuts to India's fuel-export taxes and a rebound in Middle East crude deliveries to India, which hit 11.3 million tonnes in September, the highest since February, as signs India can step back into the export market.
claims.source: Reuters (Gavin Maguire commentary; reprinted by The Hindu Business Line)

claims.text: Crux Investor reported on Oct 1 that Chinese refiners had suspended refined-product exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau with no stated end date, sending December Brent futures up 2.4% to $100.36 a barrel while the expiring November contract settled at $103.50. The report noted Middle East crude exports had recovered to 17.5 million b/d, 98% of prewar levels, even as US distillate inventories fell 2.3 million barrels to 105.2 million, 14% below the five-year average. The export suspension was corroborated by a Reuters columnist on Oct 5.

Gasoline inventories at state-owned majors fell 2.9 percent in a week to their lowest since 2022 and diesel stocks hit a 15-month low after a 2.4 percent drop, per commodity research firm JLC International cited by Bloomberg. Energy Aspects analyst Jiana Sun told Bloomberg there is a growing risk Beijing caps monthly clean product exports at about 1.2 million tons in the fourth quarter.

Energy News Beat (Sep 13, 2026) reported the second batch of 2026 clean-product export quotas brought China's total 2026 allocation to about 32 million tonnes. August product exports hit 6.01 million tonnes, up 12.7% year on year, but January to August exports were still down 9.6% year on year, with gasoline down 57% year to date, consistent with a policy-managed surplus rather than an unconstrained export boom.

General Administration of Customs (GAC) data reported by IDNFinancials (Sep 18, 2026) gave August per-fuel detail: gasoline exports 700,000 tonnes, down 17.5% year on year but the highest since October 2025; diesel 1.33 million tonnes, up 42.1% year on year and the highest since March 2024; jet fuel a record 2.55 million tonnes, up 41.4% year on year. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports fell 17.8% year on year to 5.16 million tonnes.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 28, citing Vortexa data reported by Bloomberg, that freight on the main Atlantic to Asia crude routes has eased by about $10 a barrel from the first week of October, when US Gulf Coast to South Korea shipping topped $42 a barrel, Brazil to China topped $39 and West Africa to China topped $32. A supertanker voyage from the US to Asia still cost about $60 million last week, and Asian refiners are ordering little US crude for November delivery at those rates.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 9 that record-high freight costs have effectively shut the US Gulf to Asia crude arbitrage, with Asian refiners turning to more barrels from the Middle East and South America, shipbrokers and traders told Reuters. Trafigura chartered a supertanker to ship crude from the US Gulf Coast to China at a lump-sum fee of $76 million, a source told CNBC, about ten times the $7 to $10 million before the war, implying freight costs of about $38 per barrel. Rates on the US Gulf to Japan route are also surging, with one supertanker offered at $82 million, up 50% from three weeks earlier, Bloomberg reported. With the US-Asia arbitrage closed, Asian refiners are considering more of the UAE's Murban grade, pushing its premium over Dubai quotes above $11 per barrel on Thursday.

Baltic Exchange data put the time charter equivalent for a 270,000-ton very large crude carrier (VLCC) on the TD3C Middle East Gulf to China route at about 1.212 million dollars per day on Sep 17, up from about 1.034 million the day before and roughly 700,000 at the start of September. The Baltic's Sep 18 weekly report put TD3C at Worldscale 1,140, the Gulf of Oman to China TD34 route at 870,947 dollars per day, and West Africa to China TD15 at 524,575 dollars per day.

The 2016-built VLCC Kuwait Prosperity, operated by Sinokor, was fixed at Worldscale 1,350 for a Persian Gulf to east voyage loading by Total Singapore on Sep 22, with a daily equivalent estimated above 1 million dollars. Analysts attribute the spike to reduced Hormuz transits, longer voyages via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, and diversions around the Cape of Good Hope adding an estimated 11 to 14 million dollars per voyage in charter costs alone.
claims.vintage: Fixture for Sep 22 loading; reported Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: Tide Signal News (Sep 23, 2026, citing Reuters/Baltic Exchange data) reported very large crude carrier (VLCC) freight from the Gulf of Oman to China hit Worldscale 450, about $11.50 per barrel, a record for the route and up roughly 65% from the Sep 4 TD34 assessment, as conflict risk shrank the pool of tankers willing to trade around the Gulf.

China's National Bureau of Statistics data, released Nov 16 and reported by Shanghai Metals Market, showed crude oil processing of 58.3 million tons in October, down 8.1 percent from a year earlier. The October volume works out to roughly 13.7 million barrels per day, in line with the 13.75 million barrels per day that Energy Aspects estimated for October in Reuters reporting on Nov 10, and below September levels as state refiners held back amid uncertainty over product export policy.
claims.source: National Bureau of Statistics (via Shanghai Metals Market)

claims.text: The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) reported on Nov 5 that reduced crude oil stockpiling accounted for 47 percent of the year-on-year drop in China's crude imports between March and August 2026, as temporary adjustments cushioned the Hormuz import shock. Electric vehicles displaced 38 million tonnes of oil equivalent in March to August 2026, equivalent to around 13 percent of China's crude oil imports in the same period of 2025, and growth in non-fossil generation reduced coal and gas requirements, saving an estimated $9.1 billion in fossil fuel imports since 2020, more than any other country, CREA said. Its analysis is based on National Bureau of Statistics data for domestic fuel production, refinery throughput and oil product output, and General Administration of Customs import and export volumes.
claims.source: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA)

claims.text: Reuters reported on Oct 6 that Shandong refinery utilization fell to about 55% by late September from nearly 60% at the start of the month, per consultancy Horizon Insights, as margins deteriorated after China capped fuel price increases while crude feedstock costs surged. Refiners were losing 250 to 500 yuan per metric ton by late September, compared with profits of about 500 yuan per ton in early September. One trader said buyers were unwilling to pay spot premiums above $20 a barrel. Kpler senior analyst Muyu Xu said inventories at some Shandong teapots could run out as early as the end of October and that refiners need to secure alternative supplies to avoid shutting down or cutting run rates significantly.

The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air's August 2026 snapshot (published Sep 17, 2026) found refinery throughput down 6.9% year on year in August, though recovered from July's slump. New energy vehicle (NEV) output rose 21.9% year on year to 61% of all vehicles produced, and battery production surged 70% year on year, consistent with continued structural gasoline displacement.
claims.source: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air

claims.text: Signal Ocean analysis published by Cyprus Shipping News on Nov 3, drawing on Chinese customs (GACC) and National Bureau of Statistics data, put China's September crude imports at 9.03 million barrels per day (b/d), broadly flat on August, while refinery runs climbed to 13.99 million b/d, the highest since March, so China drew on stocks for the fourth time in five months, a net 0.60 million b/d after crude exports. Of the 121.5 million barrels built by April, only 31 million remained, and at the May to September draw pace of 0.59 million b/d that remainder would be gone by late November, Signal Ocean said. Arrivals picked up in October, but those cargoes were bought in the summer, and with Brent around $100 since early September the refill is likely to slow. China was still buying from the Atlantic, with 19 very large crude carriers fixed from Brazil and West Africa to China in the last ten days of October, most of them loading in November.
claims.source: Cyprus Shipping News (Signal Ocean analysis; GACC and NBS data)

claims.text: OilPrice.com reported on Oct 22, summarizing Reuters calculations, that China drew about 530,000 barrels per day from inventories in September, the fourth draw in five months, while still holding an estimated at least 1.2 billion barrels in commercial and strategic stocks. October imports above 10 million barrels per day would reduce the need to draw on those stocks.

The weak September arrivals forced the largest draw on China's onshore crude inventories in the trackers' records: Vortexa counted a 57 million barrel draw in September and Kpler a 47.5 million barrel draw, the biggest monthly declines since their series began in 2019 and 2017 respectively, Reuters reported on Oct 14. Vortexa's Emma Li attributed the draw to Middle East shipping disruptions, mainly ship-to-ship transfer bottlenecks around Hormuz, delaying cargoes due in late August and September. Kpler pegged China's fourth-quarter seaborne crude imports at 8.0 to 8.5 million barrels per day.

The US Energy Information Administration (EIA), in analysis published April 2026, classifies China's strategic oil inventories at an estimated 1.397 billion barrels, comprising about 360 million barrels government-held and 1 billion barrels commercial. The EIA treats both as strategic because China's national oil companies have reportedly been instructed since 2024 to hold emergency oil in commercial tanks.

Geospatial firm Kayrros, via MEXC reporting from the Asia Pacific Petroleum Conference (APPEC) in Singapore, estimated China's strategic petroleum reserve (SPR) at about 415 million barrels and commercial stocks at about 780 million barrels in early September 2026, up close to 130 million barrels combined since late March, with above-ground capacity use near 60.5%, leaving room for further builds.
claims.vintage: Estimate: early Sep 2026; reported from APPEC; accessed 2026-09-24
claims.source: MEXC (citing Kayrros chief analyst Antoine Halff at APPEC)
